cards.explanation: The answer is Jerusalem, friends. God says, "…take a brick, place it before you, and draw on it the city of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 4:1) Ezekiel is a prophet, and the first thing he gets is a drawing job. I've stamped a lot of cookies, but nobody ever handed me a brick and said "make it look like a city."

The answer is True, friends. God says, "Construct a siege wall, build a ramp to it, set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it on all sides." (Ezekiel 4:2) So Ezekiel is building a whole little battle scene. On a brick. I think that's the most detailed work order anybody ever got.

The answer is a sign, friends. God says of the siege, "This will be a sign to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 4:3) Ezekiel turns his face toward the city on the brick and besieges it. The iron plate he sets up as an iron wall is part of it too.

The answer is on his right side, friends. God says, "…lie down again, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah." (Ezekiel 4:6) First it was the left side for the house of Israel, now the right side for Judah. Ezekiel is getting a full rotation, and I think he'd have paid good money for a pillow.

The answer is False, friends. God says, "I have assigned to you 40 days, a day for each year." (Ezekiel 4:6) So each day stands for a year, not a week. The same pattern works for the 390 days on the left side (Ezekiel 4:5).

The answer is prophesy against it, friends. God says, "You must turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against it." (Ezekiel 4:7) The bared arm and the steady face go with the words he speaks. Ezekiel gets the whole message across, and I'd say that's a pretty full-body sermon.

The answer is ropes, friends. God says, "Now behold, I will tie you up with ropes so you cannot turn from side to side until you have finished the days of your siege." (Ezekiel 4:8) So Ezekiel isn't left to flip over on his own. I think that takes the snooze-button temptation right out.

The answer is a single container, friends. God says, "put them in a single container and make them into bread for yourself." (Ezekiel 4:9) Wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt all go in together. In my bakery I keep my toppings in separate bowls, so this would give me a twitch.
The answer is False, friends. God says, "…you are to eat it at set times." (Ezekiel 4:10) The amount is weighed out and the timing is set too. That's a strict schedule, and I'd be in trouble with it.

The answer is in the nations He will banish them to, friends. The LORD says, "This is how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I will banish them." (Ezekiel 4:13) So the bread Ezekiel eats is a picture of how the Israelites will eat. It's a heavy picture, and the verse doesn't dress it up.

The answer is True, friends. Ezekiel says, "Ah, Lord GOD, I have never defiled myself." (Ezekiel 4:14) He goes on to say that from his youth until now he hasn't eaten anything found dead or mauled by wild beasts, and no unclean meat has entered his mouth. He speaks up plainly, and I respect that.

The answer is what he bakes his bread over, friends. God replies, "I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that." (Ezekiel 4:15) So the fuel changes, and everything else stays. Ezekiel spoke up and God answered him, and I think that's worth noticing.

The answer is weight, friends. God says, "They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight…" (Ezekiel 4:16) That matches Ezekiel's own food, which he weighs out each day (Ezekiel 4:10). In Jerusalem it comes with anxiety, and I think that's a hard way to eat.

The answer is iniquity, friends. God says, "they will be appalled at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity." (Ezekiel 4:17) The same word has been all through this passage, like when Ezekiel bears the iniquity of the house of Israel (Ezekiel 4:4-5). It's a heavy ending.
